title: Sour
intro: This is a victory lap that cannot stop answering its enemies. Jack begins above the whole earth, then spends most of the song addressing people he says are beneath his notice. The grievance eventually becomes specific: rivals protect one another and exchange opportunities, while he claims a superiority that needs none of their approval. Yet the song keeps demanding that they acknowledge it. That friction—wanting recognition while scorning the people who distribute it—gives the insults their energy. The final boast is both a celebration and a way to end an argument that 'ignoring you' has failed to end.
reading: Recognition versus refusal; a music-scene grievance staged as sovereign self-sufficiency, not a literal feud report.

revisions.editorial-1-free-flight: The opening puts him in the position of someone who can see everything without being reached. But that freedom lasts only three lines before 'you' intrudes. The song never supplies a named opponent; it supplies the irritating fact of an opponent who still occupies his attention. Read the flight against the hook: being above someone socially does not make it easy to stop arguing with them. This is swagger with an unresolved dependency underneath it, not a calm description of having moved on.
revisions.sour-book: These three objects belong together: a book, its title, its words. The target is being reduced to something they have written or presented to the world, then that work is described as spoiled, exhausted and insecure. The insults refuse to debate its contents; they discredit the person through the writing. The pencil that soon becomes a weapon keeps this quarrel inside a world of words and judgments. That is stronger evidence for a dispute over expression and status than for any particular critic, publication or named rival.
revisions.editorial-1-refusal-loop: He gives three different reasons for not acknowledging the opponent: contempt, unfamiliarity and dislike. Those reasons do not have to add up; each is another door slammed in the other person's face. But the repeated 'I ignore you' also makes sure the refusal is heard. The hook is an active humiliation, not an absence of contact. When he follows it with 'this is my game,' he claims the right to decide whose presence counts at all. The song wants the rewards of winning the contest and the freedom to say the contestants do not matter.
revisions.editorial-1-resource-swap: This is where the contempt acquires a concrete object: people forming a circle and trading access. The preceding 'huddling for warmth' could describe friendship in a sympathetic song; here 'losers' and 'trash' recast it as mutual protection for people whose work cannot stand alone. His counterclaim is that he came first through his own ability. The next song, 'Blessed,' warmly values a circle of friends and family, so the distinction is not solitude versus all human connection. It is earned affection versus belonging treated as a currency.
revisions.sour-cards: The supposed revelation comes after he has already repeated that he is exceptionally good. There is no new information to disclose. What changes is the posture: he stops explaining why the others are worthless and allows himself the pleasure of saying he is great. That makes the ending an escape from the hook's exhausting list of reasons. It also makes the boast knowingly theatrical—the grand mask-removal reveals the same bragging speaker who has been there all along.
